source_refs.note: Chapter 28 exercise (PDF 183-185) solved: 10 MCQs keyed from the chapter (no key printed), 10 short, 3 constructed response (Rf values and GC % worked from the printed chromatograms) and 3 descriptive questions. Book corrections: MCQ II, VIII, Q2(b), Q3.

blocks.prompt: I) Why must the solvent level be below the spot of the dye?

options.text: To prevent the dye from dissolving directly into the solvent

blocks.explanation: If the spot were below the solvent level, the dye would simply dissolve away into the solvent in the tank instead of moving up the paper and separating (28.2).

blocks.prompt: II) Why do some components of a dye travel further up the paper than others?

options.text: They are more soluble in the water trap in paper (stationary phase)
They are more soluble in the solvent (mobile phase)

blocks.explanation: Components more soluble in the solvent (mobile phase) move further up; those that dissolve better in the water trapped in the paper (stationary phase) do not travel far (28.2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (a) is printed 'the water trap in paper'; it means the water trapped in the paper.

blocks.prompt: III) A substance has a very low Rf value. What does this indicate?

options.text: It is insoluble in the solvent
It is highly soluble in the solvent
It strongly sticks to the water inside paper

blocks.explanation: Rf = distance travelled by the substance / distance travelled by the solvent. A low Rf means it moved very little because it is held strongly by (dissolves better in) the water of the paper, the stationary phase (28.2).

blocks.prompt: IV) Which statement best explains adsorption?

options.text: Substance sticks only to the surface of another material

blocks.explanation: Adsorption is a surface phenomenon in which particles accumulate only on the outer surface, e.g. activated charcoal adsorbs gases (28.1).

blocks.prompt: V) A polar compound in TLC will usually:
blocks.explanation: Polar substances are attracted more strongly to the polar stationary phase (alumina or silica) and are adsorbed more strongly, so they travel slowly and stay near the baseline (28.3).

blocks.prompt: VI) Why is TLC considered faster than paper chromatography?

options.text: It has a solid stationary phase that allows quicker separation

blocks.explanation: TLC uses a thin solid layer of alumina or silica as the stationary phase, which separates by adsorption and solubility and is faster than paper chromatography (28.3, 28.5).

blocks.prompt: VII) What is the role of the carrier gas in gas chromatography?

options.text: To carry vaporized sample through the column

blocks.explanation: The carrier gas (an inert gas such as helium or nitrogen) is the mobile phase; it carries the vapours of the sample through the column (28.4).

blocks.prompt: VIII) Why must the stationary phase in GC have a high boiling point?

options.text: To remain in liquid form during the process

blocks.explanation: The stationary phase is a non-volatile, high-boiling liquid on silica or alumina particles. It must stay liquid in the hot column and not evaporate and be carried away by the carrier gas (28.4).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book labels the last two options c) and c); the fourth option, 'To react with gases', should be d). The answer is the first c), 'To remain in liquid form during the process'.

blocks.prompt: IX) What does the area under a peak in a chromatogram indicate?
blocks.explanation: The area of each peak gives the proportion of that component in the mixture; area of a peak = ½ × base × height (28.4).

blocks.prompt: X) If two peaks have similar base width but different heights, how can composition be estimated?
blocks.explanation: When peaks are very narrow or have similar base widths, peak height is used instead of area to estimate the proportion of the components (28.4).

blocks.prompt: a) What is the principle of paper chromatography?
blocks.explanation: Partition (relative solubility): the components of the sample are shared between the stationary phase (water held by the cellulose of the paper) and the mobile phase (solvent). Components more soluble in the solvent move further; those more soluble in the water move less, so they separate (28.2, 28.5).

blocks.prompt: b) Why is pencil used instead of ink in chromatography to mark the basline?
blocks.explanation: Pencil (graphite) does not dissolve in the solvent, so the line stays where it is. Ink is itself a mixture of dyes; it would dissolve, move up with the solvent and give extra spots that mix with the sample's spots.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints 'basline'; the word is baseline.

blocks.prompt: c) State two advantages of TLC over paper chromatography.
blocks.explanation:
1. TLC is faster than paper chromatography.
2. Its solid stationary phase (silica or alumina) separates by both adsorption and solubility, giving quicker separation; colourless spots can be located by UV light or iodine vapour as well as by sprays (28.3, 28.5).

blocks.prompt: d) Why do polar substances move slowly in TLC?
blocks.explanation: The stationary phase (alumina or silica) is polar. Polar substances are attracted to it more strongly and are adsorbed more, so they move slowly and have low Rf values (28.3).

blocks.prompt: e) Why is TLC not suitable for large-scale separation?
blocks.explanation: In TLC only small amounts of sample can be applied to the thin layer and analysed, so it cannot separate large quantities (28.3).

blocks.prompt: f) What is the function of injector port in GC?
blocks.explanation: The sample is injected into the injector port, where it is quickly vaporised by the oven; the vapour then enters the carrier gas stream and goes into the column (28.4).

blocks.prompt: g) Why must samples be volatile in GC?
blocks.explanation: The mobile phase in GC is a gas, so the sample must be in the gaseous (vapour) state to be carried through the column. Substances that do not vaporise easily, e.g. proteins and polymers, cannot be analysed (28.4).

blocks.prompt: h) State two limitations of gas chromatography.
blocks.explanation:
1. GC works only for volatile (easily vaporised) substances.
2. Samples must be thermally stable; compounds that decompose at high temperature cannot be used. (Also, instruments and maintenance are costly.) (28.4)

blocks.prompt: i) What information does a chromatogram provide?
blocks.explanation:
1. The number of peaks shows the number of components.
2. The retention time of each peak helps identify the component.
3. The area (or height) of each peak gives the proportion of that component in the mixture (28.4).

blocks.prompt: j) What is adsorption? Give one example.
blocks.explanation: Adsorption is a surface phenomenon in which particles accumulate only on the outer surface of another material. Example: activated charcoal adsorbs gases and impurities on its surface, so it is used in filters (28.1).

blocks.prompt:
a) A mixture of amino acids is analysed using thin layer chromatography. The chromatogram obtained is shown. The table shows some Rf values for different amino acids in the same solvent.
(Chromatogram: baseline at 0 cm, solvent front at 5.0 cm; spot A at about 3.55 cm and spot B at about 1.45 cm. Table of Rf values: alanine 0.40, glutamic acid 0.29, leucine 0.71, valine 0.61.)
I) Use the chromatogram and the Rf values to deduce the amino acid responsible for spot A and spot B.
ii) A second chromatogram of the same mixture is taken using a more polar solvent. Predict the effect on the Rf values of the amino acids. Explain your reasoning.
blocks.explanation:
I) Given: distance moved by the solvent = 5.0 cm; spot A ≈ 3.55 cm; spot B ≈ 1.45 cm (read from the scale)
Formula: Rf = distance travelled by the substance / distance travelled by the solvent
Spot A: Rf = 3.55 cm / 5.0 cm = 0.71 → leucine (Rf 0.71)
Spot B: Rf = 1.45 cm / 5.0 cm = 0.29 → glutamic acid (Rf 0.29)
ii) The Rf values increase (the spots move further from the baseline). Amino acids are polar, so they dissolve better in a more polar mobile phase, and a polar solvent also competes with them for the polar stationary phase, so they are held less strongly and travel further with the solvent (28.3). Rf values must therefore be compared only for the same solvent.

blocks.prompt:
3. Gas chromatography involves a stationary phase and a mobile phase.
a) Name a suitable substance that could be used for each phase.
b) A mixture of three organic compounds is separated by gas chromatography. The chromatogram obtained is shown below.
(Chromatogram: detector response against time/min, four peaks in order of time labelled ester A, ester B, ester C and ester D, marked 14, 25, 52 and 38 respectively; the peaks have similar base widths.)
I) Explain the meaning of the term retention time.
ii) Calculate the % of N in the mixture. Show your working.
blocks.explanation:
a) Mobile phase: an inert carrier gas such as helium (or nitrogen).
Stationary phase: a non-volatile, long-chain hydrocarbon liquid of high boiling point coated on small particles of silica (SiO₂) or alumina (Al₂O₃) (28.4).
b) I) Retention time is the time taken by a substance to pass through the column, from injection until its peak is recorded by the detector. Each substance has its own retention time under the same conditions, so it helps to identify it (28.4).
ii) The peaks have similar base widths, so peak height can be used instead of area (28.4). Taking the printed numbers as the relative peak sizes:
Given: A = 14, B = 25, C = 52, D = 38
Sum = 14 + 25 + 52 + 38 = 129
Formula: % of a component = (its peak / sum of all peaks) × 100
% A = 14/129 × 100 = 10.9 %
% B = 25/129 × 100 = 19.4 %
% C = 52/129 × 100 = 40.3 %
% D = 38/129 × 100 = 29.5 %
The largest component is ester C (40.3 %); the smallest is ester A (10.9 %).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Part b) speaks of 'three organic compounds' but the chromatogram shows four peaks, labelled ester A, B, C and D; and ii) asks for the '% of N', but no component N is labelled. The working above gives the percentage of every ester, so the intended one can be read off. The book does not say whether 14, 25, 52 and 38 are heights or areas; with similar base widths the result is the same.

blocks.prompt:
c) An unknown amino acid is analysed by thin-layer chromatography. Two chromatographs of the unknown amino acid and four reference amino acids, P, Q, R and S, are obtained using two different solvents. Identify the unknown amino acid. Justify your answer.
(Both plates: baseline 0 cm, solvent front 5.0 cm. Solvent 1: unknown about 1.7 cm, P about 0.75 cm, Q about 1.7 cm, R about 3.25 cm, S about 1.7 cm. Solvent 2: unknown about 3.75 cm, P about 1.1 cm, Q about 2.5 cm, R about 3.75 cm, S about 3.75 cm.)
blocks.explanation:
The unknown is S.
Solvent 1: the unknown spot (≈ 1.7 cm, Rf ≈ 1.7/5.0 = 0.34) is level with Q and S, so it could be Q or S, but not P or R.
Solvent 2: the unknown spot (≈ 3.75 cm, Rf ≈ 3.75/5.0 = 0.75) is level with R and S, so it could be R or S, but not P or Q.
Only S has the same Rf value as the unknown in both solvents, so the unknown amino acid is S. Two solvents are used because two substances can have the same Rf value in one solvent (Q and S in solvent 1; R and S in solvent 2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The parts of Q3 are numbered a), 3. and c) as printed; the second part, '3.', should be b). Inside it the sub-parts restart at a), b), and the numbering mixes I) and ii).

blocks.prompt: Q4. Describe the principle and working of paper chromatography.
blocks.explanation:
Principle: partition, i.e. relative solubility. The paper's cellulose holds water, which is the stationary phase; the solvent is the mobile phase. Each component is shared between the two: components more soluble in the solvent move further up the paper, those more soluble in the water move less, so they separate (28.2).
Working:
1. Draw a baseline in pencil near the bottom of the chromatography paper.
2. Put a small spot of the sample on the baseline with a capillary tube.
3. Place the paper in a tank containing a suitable solvent so that the solvent level is below the spot; cover the tank with a lid.
4. The solvent soaks up the paper; the components dissolve in it to different extents and move up different distances.
5. When the solvent is near the top, take out the paper, mark the solvent front and let it dry.
6. Colourless components are made visible by spraying a locating agent.
7. Measure the distances and calculate Rf for each spot:
Rf = distance travelled by the substance / distance travelled by the solvent (no unit)
8. Identify components by comparing Rf values with standards under the same conditions (same solvent and temperature).
Paper chromatography separates both coloured and colourless substances and needs only a very small quantity of the mixture, e.g. the pigments of leaves (Figure 28.1).

blocks.prompt: Q5. Explain the principle and working process of thin layer chromatography (TLC) in detail.
blocks.explanation:
Principle: adsorption together with solubility. The stationary phase is a thin solid layer of alumina (Al₂O₃) or silica (SiO₂); the mobile phase is a liquid solvent. Polar substances are attracted more to the polar solid and are adsorbed strongly, so they move slowly; non-polar substances are more soluble in a non-polar solvent and move further up (28.3).
Working:
1. Mix alumina or silica with water to make a slurry, spread it evenly on a glass slide and dry it in an oven to get a white solid layer.
2. Draw a straight baseline in pencil near the bottom; put spots of the samples on it with a capillary tube (more than one sample can be spotted).
3. Stand the slide in the solvent in a chromatography tank, with the baseline above the solvent level; cover with a lid.
4. The solvent rises; each component is adsorbed and dissolved to a different extent, so the components separate.
5. Remove the slide when the solvent has risen far enough, mark the solvent front and dry it.
6. Locate colourless spots: ninhydrin spray gives purple spots with amino acids; some substances glow in UV light; some turn brown with iodine vapour.
7. Calculate Rf values and compare them with standard values to identify the components.
Applications: identifying unknown compounds, checking purity, following the progress of a reaction, testing drugs and food additives, detecting pollutants and pesticides, and forensic work.
Limitations: mainly qualitative; poor separation of compounds with close Rf values; only small amounts; sensitive to humidity, temperature and cleanliness.

blocks.prompt: Q6. Describe the main components of gas chromatography.
blocks.explanation:
Main components of a gas chromatograph (Figure 28.5):
1. Carrier gas supply (mobile phase): an inert gas such as helium or nitrogen that carries the sample vapours through the column.
2. Injector port (in the injector oven): the sample is injected here and quickly vaporised, then swept into the column by the carrier gas.
3. Column (in the column oven): a long coiled tube (1-5 m long, 3-6 mm diameter) packed with tiny silica particles of large surface area, coated with the stationary phase, a non-volatile, high-boiling, long-chain hydrocarbon liquid. Here separation occurs: substances that interact more strongly with the stationary phase move more slowly.
4. Detector (in the detector oven): identifies the separated substances as they leave the column and records the retention time of each.
5. Recorder or computer: shows the signals as peaks on a graph, the chromatogram. The retention time identifies each component and the peak area (½ × base × height) gives its proportion.
Then the gas goes to the exit.
